Numerical experiments on a serial queuing system and a 2000-dimensional optimization problem demonstrate the superior performance and scalability of MGS.
tldr: This paper proposes a min-max gradient search algorithm for constrained simulation optimization, with finite-time convergence guarantees.
motivation: Constrained simulation optimization is challenging due to noisy gradient estimates and lack of analytical gradients for constraints.
method: The algorithm integrates a primal-dual framework with stochastic gradient estimators, performing alternating gradient descent and ascent on primal and dual variables.
result: The algorithm achieves a finite-time convergence rate to a stationary point, demonstrated on a queuing system and a high-dimensional problem.
conclusion: The proposed MGS method is efficient and scalable for constrained simulation optimization problems.

title: Lacunary Series, Nonlinear Functionals And Banach Space Structure
authors: Istvan Berkes, Eduard Stefanescu, Robert Tichy
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a previous paper we studied the asymptotic behavior of [MATH] for lacunary sequences [MATH] of random variables in [MATH] and used the result to give a necessary and sufficient condition for the first alternative in the Kadec-Pe{\l}czynski theorem in the case [MATH]. In the present paper we extend this result for nonlinear functionals [MATH], establishing a uniform version of the subsequence principle of Aldous . Moreover, we prove Kadec-Pe{\l}czynski type theorems in Orlicz spaces [MATH].
tldr: The paper studies lacunary series and nonlinear functionals in Banach spaces, proving Kadec-Pełczyński type theorems in Orlicz spaces.
motivation: To extend previous results on asymptotic behavior of lacunary sequences to nonlinear functionals and to establish uniform versions of the subsequence principle.
method: Uses probabilistic and functional analytic techniques, including martingale methods and Banach space geometry.
result: Proves a uniform version of Aldous' subsequence principle and Kadec-Pełczyński type theorems in Orlicz spaces.
conclusion: The results contribute to the theory of lacunary series and Banach space structure, but have no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Constructing $c^1$ Limit Surfaces From Unstructured Splines Via Averaging And Refinement
authors: Thomas Takacs Syeda Hijab Zahra
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we present a construction for unstructured splines over quadrilateral meshes by iterative averaging and refinement. We represent the spline as a multi-patch B-spline, where the degrees of freedom are those B-spline coefficients on the quadrilateral patches that are not associated with interior edges and vertices of the mesh, i.e., their corresponding Greville points lie inside the patches. In every averaging step, we replace the remaining B-spline coefficients associated with interior edges and vertices by suitable averages of neighboring degrees of freedom. In the refinement step we apply regular splits to all patches by knot insertion. This process results in a subdivision scheme that, for degree [MATH], is similar to the almost-[MATH] spline construction from (Takacs, Toshniwal. CMAME, 2023) and behaves similar to Doo-Sabin subdivision, cf. (Doo, Sabin. CAD, 1978), and that can be defined for arbitrary degrees and regularities inside the patches. We derive two families of spline constructions, based on simple and coplanar averaging, respectively, and analyze their spectral properties when interpreted as subdivision schemes. Using this interpretation, we show that they are [MATH] in the limit. Moreover, the coplanar averaging scheme produces splines that are [MATH] at all vertices for every level of refinement, whereas the simple averaging is [MATH] only in the limit. For both constructions, we have control over the subdominant eigenvalue, which has multiplicity two and can range between [MATH] and [MATH], with [MATH] often being the desired option. The resulting basis functions form a partition of unity. Moreover, they form a non-negative partition of unity for suitably selected averaging parameters.
tldr: This paper presents a construction for unstructured splines over quadrilateral meshes using iterative averaging and refinement, producing C1 limit surfaces.
motivation: To develop a spline construction that works on unstructured quadrilateral meshes with arbitrary degree and regularity, achieving C1 continuity in the limit.
method: The spline is represented as a multi-patch B-spline; degrees of freedom are coefficients not associated with interior edges/vertices. Averaging replaces interior coefficients by averages of neighboring degrees of freedom, followed by refinement via knot insertion.
result: Two families of constructions (simple and coplanar averaging) are derived, both producing C1 limit surfaces. The coplanar averaging scheme yields C1 at all vertices for every refinement level, while simple averaging is C1 only in the limit. The subdominant eigenvalue has multiplicity two and can be tuned.
conclusion: The resulting basis functions form a non-negative partition of unity for suitable parameters, and the construction generalizes Doo-Sabin subdivision to arbitrary degrees.

title: Structure-Preserving Discontinuous Galerkin Methods For Stochastic Shallow Water Equations
authors: Yekaterina Epshteyn, Akil Narayan, Yinqian Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shallow water equations (SWE) are fundamental models in fluid dynamics that are essential for studying a wide range of geophysical and engineering phenomena. In many practical applications, uncertainties arising from initial conditions and bottom topography must be taken into account, motivating the development of stable and accurate numerical methods for stochastic SWE. Building on the hyperbolicity-preserving stochastic Galerkin formulation for SWE [Dai, Epshteyn, Narayan, 2021 SISC] and a stochastic extension of the entropy stable discontinuous Galerkin methods for skew-symmetric SWE [Fu, 2022 JSC], we develop a structure-preserving, entropy conservative, and entropy stable discontinuous Galerkin--stochastic Galerkin method for the stochastic shallow water system, with the well-balanced property. We demonstrate the accuracy, applicability, and robustness of the proposed structure-preserving algorithms through several numerical experiments.
tldr: This paper develops structure-preserving numerical methods for stochastic shallow water equations, which are unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Shallow water equations are important for geophysical and engineering applications, and uncertainties in initial conditions and bottom topography require robust numerical methods.
method: The authors combine a hyperbolicity-preserving stochastic Galerkin formulation with entropy stable discontinuous Galerkin methods to create a structure-preserving, entropy conservative, and well-balanced numerical scheme.
result: Numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, applicability, and robustness of the proposed algorithms.
conclusion: The proposed methods provide stable and accurate simulations for stochastic shallow water systems, but have no connection to the user's research interests.

title: Spectral Decomposition Of $(\star,\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)$-structured Matrix Polynomials With Arbitrary Degree And Its Applications
authors: Shifang Yuan Kang Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper provides the spectral decompositions of [MATH]-structured matrix polynomials [MATH] in the unified form by a standard pair and parameter matrix. Using the recursive relationship between the coefficient matrices of [MATH], equivalent expressions of these coefficient matrices are provided. And then the spectral decomposition is applied to solve the inverse eigenvalue problem and the eigenvalue embedding problem with no spill-over.
tldr: This paper presents spectral decompositions of structured matrix polynomials and applies them to inverse eigenvalue and eigenvalue embedding problems.
motivation: To provide a unified spectral decomposition for a class of structured matrix polynomials and solve related inverse problems with no spill-over.
method: Uses standard pairs and parameter matrices, leveraging recursive relationships between coefficient matrices to derive equivalent expressions.
result: Obtains spectral decompositions in a unified form and applies them to inverse eigenvalue and eigenvalue embedding problems.
conclusion: The proposed method effectively solves the targeted inverse problems, demonstrating the utility of the spectral decomposition.

title: Adjoint-based Perfusion Estimation From Dynamic Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound: Advection-Diffusion And Two-Compartment Models
authors: Sophie Externbrink, Ahmed El Kaffas, Dimitre Hristov, Sebastian G\"otschel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tumor perfusion and vascular properties are important determinants of a cancer's response to therapy. In this paper, we discuss the estimation of spatially varying blood flow velocities and perfusion parameters from time-resolved contrast agent concentration data. We compare a standard parabolic advection-diffusion model against a two-compartment model governed by a coupled system of hyperbolic advection-reaction equations, which is physiologically more sound. To address the inherent ill-posedness of this parameter identification problem, we employ Tikhonov regularization and derive continuous adjoint equations necessary for efficient, gradient-based minimization. We discuss the numerical discretization of the state and adjoint systems using state-of-the-art schemes, and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed reconstruction algorithms through numerical experiments on synthetic data and in vivo dynamic contrast-enhanced ultrasound measurements.
tldr: This paper presents adjoint-based methods for estimating tumor perfusion parameters from dynamic contrast-enhanced ultrasound using advection-diffusion and two-compartment models.
motivation: Tumor perfusion and vascular properties are key determinants of cancer therapy response, and accurate estimation from medical imaging is clinically important.
method: The authors formulate parameter identification as an ill-posed inverse problem, employ Tikhonov regularization, and derive continuous adjoint equations for efficient gradient-based minimization.
result: Numerical experiments on synthetic data and in vivo ultrasound measurements demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed reconstruction algorithms.
conclusion: The two-compartment model is physiologically more sound and yields improved perfusion estimates compared to the standard advection-diffusion model.

title: Constraint-driven Optimization And Parametrization Of Industrial Nurbs Geometries Via Neural Deformation Field
authors: Federico Tamburlin, Giovanni Canali, Giuseppe Alessio D'inverno, Nicola Demo, Andrea Mola, Gianluigi Rozza
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents a differentiable framework for the parametrization and shape optimization of industrial CAD geometries represented by multi-patch NURBS surfaces. The method enables the deformation of complex CAD models through a physics-informed geometric parametrization, allowing direct morphing driven by physical constraints without the need to prescribe a predefined deformation strategy. A neural displacement field, implemented as a multi-layer perceptron acting on the NURBS control points, provides a compact parametrization of the admissible design space while preserving patch connectivity. Global geometric quantities relevant to hydrostatic design, including displaced volume, wetted surface area and buoyancy centroid, are formulated as differentiable integral operators evaluated on the parametric domain. These quantities are computed through Gauss-Legendre quadrature combined with analytical B-spline derivatives for surface metric evaluation, allowing gradient propagation to the deformation parameters while limiting the computational overhead of automatic differentiation. The proposed framework operates directly on CAD representations without intermediate mesh generation. Numerical experiments on a modified KVLCC2 hull demonstrate the capability of the method to satisfy competing hydrostatic constraints while producing smooth CAD-compatible geometries and showing stable convergence across multiple random initializations.
tldr: A differentiable framework for shape optimization of industrial NURBS geometries using neural deformation fields, applied to hydrostatic design of a ship hull.
motivation: To enable direct, constraint-driven deformation of complex CAD models without predefined strategies or intermediate meshing.
method: A neural displacement field (MLP) deforms NURBS control points; differentiable integral operators compute hydrostatic quantities via Gauss-Legendre quadrature and analytical B-spline derivatives.
result: The method satisfies competing hydrostatic constraints on a KVLCC2 hull, producing smooth CAD-compatible geometries with stable convergence.
conclusion: The framework offers a compact, differentiable parametrization for industrial shape optimization directly on CAD representations.

title: An Adaptive Dual-Primal Isogeometric Tearing And Interconnecting (ieti-dp) Method For Solving The Biharmonic Equation Over Planar Multi-patch Geometries
authors: Mario Kapl, Alja\v{z} Kosma\v{c}, Vito Vitrih
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a novel adaptive isogeometric method for solving the biharmonic equation over planar multi-patch domains with possibly extraordinary vertices, parametrized by analysis-suitable G^1 multi-patch geometries. The proposed technique relies on the concept of Dual-Primal Isogeometric Tearing and Interconnecting (IETI-DP), which enforces the required C^1-smoothness of the solution across a common edge of two neighboring patches by imposing appropriate continuity conditions by means of Lagrange multipliers. The resulting saddle point problem is solved using a dual-primal formulation, first by a small linear problem for the Lagrange multipliers and then by local, parallelizable linear problems on the individual patches for the coefficients of the numerical solution. While for the local problems on the single patches standard diagonally scaling is used as preconditioner, a suitable preconditioner for the problem of finding the Lagrange multipliers is introduced. To perform adaptive refinement, the solution of the biharmonic equation on the single patches of the multi-patch domain is discretized by employing (truncated) hierarchical B-splines, and an appropriate refinement strategy of the underlying mesh is presented. Finally, the potential of the developed adaptive IETI-DP method for solving the biharmonic equation over planar multi-patch geometries is numerically tested on the basis of several numerical examples. Thereby, the numerical results show on the one hand optimal convergence behavior with respect to adaptive refinement, and on the other hand a good performance of the proposed preconditioner for the linear problem of determining the Lagrange multipliers.
tldr: This paper presents an adaptive isogeometric method for solving the biharmonic equation over planar multi-patch geometries using a dual-primal tearing and interconnecting approach.
motivation: The biharmonic equation arises in various applications such as thin plate bending and fluid dynamics, and efficient numerical methods for complex geometries are needed.
method: The method enforces C^1 continuity across patch interfaces via Lagrange multipliers, solves a saddle point problem with a dual-primal formulation, and uses hierarchical B-splines for adaptive refinement.
result: Numerical examples demonstrate optimal convergence rates with adaptive refinement and good performance of the proposed preconditioner for the Lagrange multiplier system.
conclusion: The adaptive IETI-DP method is effective for solving the biharmonic equation on multi-patch domains with extraordinary vertices.

title: Riesz Summability Of Dirichlet Series Generating Holomorphic Functions Of Finite Order
authors: Yarne Tranoy Andreas Debrouwere
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a frequency [MATH], we study the Riesz summability of [MATH]-Dirichlet series [MATH] generating holomorphic functions of finite order. We present a new separation condition on the frequency [MATH] ensuring that, for any [MATH], each [MATH]-Dirichlet series that is somewhere Riesz summable of some order and admits a holomorphic extension [MATH] to the right half-plane [MATH] satisfying [MATH] as [MATH] on [MATH], is in fact Riesz summable of order [MATH] on [MATH]. This extends Bohr's theorem, which corresponds to the case [MATH]. Our work improves a recent result of Defant and Schoolmann, who showed the above property under Landau's condition (LC). Along the way, we also establish novel bounds on the coefficients of such [MATH]-Dirichlet series and, under a mild condition on the frequency [MATH], show that they are optimal.
tldr: This paper studies Riesz summability of Dirichlet series generating holomorphic functions of finite order, a topic in complex analysis and number theory.
motivation: To extend Bohr's theorem on Dirichlet series summability to more general frequencies and improve upon recent results by Defant and Schoolmann.
method: The authors introduce a new separation condition on the frequency and use complex analysis techniques to prove Riesz summability properties.
result: They show that under the new condition, Dirichlet series that are somewhere Riesz summable and admit a holomorphic extension are Riesz summable on a larger domain, and they obtain optimal coefficient bounds.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of Dirichlet series summability but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: The Balance Property: The Constrained Case, With A View On Risk Sharing
authors: Mario V. W\"uthrich
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The balance property is an important property of fitted statistical models deployed for insurance pricing. It guarantees that the total actuarial price in the fitted model is equal to the totally observed loss used to fit the model. This can be seen as an in-sample global unbiasedness property. Maximum likelihood fitted generalized linear models (GLMs) with canonical links automatically fulfill the balance property. Lindholm-W\"uthrich (Scandinavian Actuarial Journal, 2026) discussed two popular balance correction methods in case the balance property fails to hold. This note extends this discussion with a third method, constrained GLM fitting, that turns out to be superior over the two previously discussed ones. Moreover, we highlight the connection between the balance property and ex-post risk sharing rules.
tldr: This paper discusses the balance property in insurance pricing models and proposes a constrained GLM fitting method for correction.
motivation: The balance property ensures unbiasedness in insurance pricing, but standard models may fail to satisfy it; existing correction methods have limitations.
method: The author introduces a constrained generalized linear model (GLM) fitting approach that enforces the balance property during estimation.
result: The constrained GLM method outperforms two previously discussed balance correction methods.
conclusion: Constrained GLM fitting is a superior technique for maintaining the balance property in insurance pricing models, with connections to risk sharing rules.

title: A Natural Decomposition Method For Essential Boundary Conditions In Noninterpolatory Meshfree Spaces
authors: Jingkai Zhang, Tiexiang Li, Shuo Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a natural decomposition method (NDM)for imposing essential boundary conditions in noninterpolatory meshfree Galerkin spaces without boundary parameter tuning or auxiliary constraint construction. In such spaces, algebraic coefficients generally do not coincide with boundary values; hence coefficient assignment or nodal boundary prescription is not equivalent to imposing the continuous trace required by the variational problem. NDM introduces boundary data before discretization through a natural transfer mechanism: a source subproblem accounts for the forcing term, a weighted curl correction transfers the remaining trace mismatch, and a scalar recovery step reconstructs the solution from the corrected weighted gradient. For topologically trivial single domains with connected boundary, the reconstructed solution is equivalent, at the continuous level, to the solution satisfying the prescribed essential boundary data. The discrete analysis separates the approximation defect of the recovery space from the upstream transfer error visible to that space. Numerical experiments on benchmark problems evaluate the proposed transfer mechanism and report the associated conditioning, computational cost, and boundary perturbation behavior.
tldr: This paper presents a numerical method for imposing essential boundary conditions in noninterpolatory meshfree Galerkin spaces.
motivation: Noninterpolatory meshfree methods suffer from the difficulty of imposing essential boundary conditions because the basis functions do not satisfy the Kronecker delta property.
method: The method decomposes the problem into a source subproblem, a weighted curl correction, and a scalar recovery step to transfer boundary data before discretization.
result: The reconstructed solution is equivalent to the solution with prescribed essential boundary data for topologically trivial single domains with connected boundary.
conclusion: The approach avoids boundary parameter tuning and auxiliary constraint construction, and numerical experiments demonstrate its effectiveness.

title: Letting Homogeneity Entropy Select S-Pairs In Buchberger's Algorithm
authors: Uzma Shafiq, Matthew England, Amirhosein Sadeghimanesh, Nayyar Zaidi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a novel S-pair selection strategy called Homogeneity Entropy, for deciding the sequence of S-polynomials to construct in Buchberger's algorithm to compute a Groebner basis. The strategy uses an information theoretic measure derived from the distribution of degrees among the monomials of the S-polynomial: a very different approach to the classical heuristics such as Degree, Normal and Sugar, or indeed the more recent machine learning approaches to the problem. We implement this strategy and evaluate it on two different datasets: (1) variations of randomly generated polynomial systems with controlled numbers of variables, degrees, and densities; and (2) the PHCpack benchmark dataset sourced from real world problems. The Homogeneity Entropy strategy significantly outperforms classical strategies on random polynomial datasets, but on the PHCpack dataset the classical strategies perform better. This suggests the right strategy varies with the shape of the data and we explore this in several experiments. The new strategy offers practically meaningful gains on certain distributions, and represents the first use of such information-theoretic guidance in the optimisation of symbolic computation algorithms.
tldr: This paper proposes a novel S-pair selection strategy for Buchberger's algorithm using an information-theoretic measure called Homogeneity Entropy, but it is in the field of symbolic computation and algebraic geometry, unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The goal is to improve the efficiency of Buchberger's algorithm for computing Groebner bases by selecting a better sequence of S-polynomials.
method: The authors introduce Homogeneity Entropy, derived from the distribution of degrees among monomials of the S-polynomial, and compare it to classical heuristics and machine learning approaches on random and benchmark datasets.
result: The Homogeneity Entropy strategy outperforms classical strategies on random polynomial datasets but performs worse on the PHCpack benchmark dataset, indicating that the best strategy depends on the data distribution.
conclusion: The new strategy offers practical gains for certain distributions and represents the first use of information-theoretic guidance in symbolic computation optimization.

title: A Temporal Spatial Minimax Rate For Smoothly-Varying Distributions In Wasserstein Space
authors: Munsik Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the minimax rate of estimating a future value [MATH] of a curve [MATH] in the [MATH]-Wasserstein space [MATH] from finitely many noisy snapshots of its past, under an adiabatic bound [MATH] on the [MATH]-th covariant derivative of the velocity field. Our central result is a unified temporal-spatial minimax lower bound: over regular, locally transport-rich subclasses, every estimator incurs [MATH]-risk with [MATH]-exponent [MATH], [MATH] ([MATH] the total sample size). It follows from a temporal-to-spatial reduction: the smoothness budget defines a reachable [MATH]-ball into which a transport packing is embedded along the time axis, and the information of the entire snapshot experiment is controlled by a Fano argument -- the spatial packing is classical, but its smoothness-admissible temporal embedding and the full-window analysis are new. The bound interpolates a dimension-free extrapolation floor of order [MATH] -- the irreducible cost of an unobserved future, present even with the exact past -- and the spatial estimation curse [MATH], recovering the static distribution-estimation rate as [MATH]. We state the lower bound in a design-dependent form -- with a design-weighted effective sample size -- valid for arbitrary observation times, and obtain the closed-form exponent in the dense (equispaced) regime. The matching upper bound is established at [MATH] (rate [MATH], [MATH]) and, in a translation submodel, for all [MATH]; for [MATH] a covariant estimator attains the rate conditionally on two estimates (a comparison-geometry bias bound and an optimal-transport map-estimation rate), leaving the unconditional general-[MATH] upper bound as an open problem. Numerical experiments on synthetic curved and flat families corroborate the predicted exponents.
tldr: This paper studies the minimax rate for estimating a future value of a curve in Wasserstein space under an adiabatic bound, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The paper addresses a problem in optimal transport and statistical estimation of smoothly varying distributions, motivated by applications in data science and probability.
method: The authors derive a temporal-spatial minimax lower bound using a Fano argument and a transport packing embedded along the time axis, and establish matching upper bounds for certain cases.
result: A unified minimax lower bound is obtained that interpolates between a dimension-free extrapolation floor and the spatial estimation curse, with closed-form exponent for equispaced observations.
conclusion: The results provide fundamental limits for predicting future distributions from noisy snapshots, but the work is purely mathematical and unrelated to the user's research interests.

title: Explicit Convergence Regions Of PID-Damped Accelerated Gradient Methods In Nonconvex Optimization
authors: Ailun Jian, Xun Li, Weigang Sun, Gaohang Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Momentum-based accelerated gradient methods are widely adopted to expedite convergence in nonconvex optimization, but are prone to overshooting and oscillatory behavior. A class of PID-damped accelerated gradient methods mitigates this issue by augmenting classical momentum methods with a discrete-time derivative damping term. However, the coupling among the step size, momentum, and derivative gain renders the explicit characterization of their convergence regions analytically intractable, leaving explicit theoretical convergence boundaries unexplored. In this paper, we model this class of algorithms as a third-order nonlinear feedback dynamical system and establish explicit three-dimensional convergence regions for the step size, momentum, and derivative gain via a robust control-theoretic analysis based on the Kalman-Yakubovich-Popov (KYP) lemma, formally guaranteeing linear convergence under the Regularity Condition. Furthermore, we reveal a strict geometric upper bound on the derivative gain dictated by the nonconvex curvature, beyond which over-damping severely contracts the feasible step-size region, providing a rigorous theoretical explanation for the overdamped stagnation phenomenon. Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical boundaries and illustrate practical parameter selection guidelines for the derivative gain.
tldr: This paper analyzes convergence regions of PID-damped accelerated gradient methods in nonconvex optimization using control theory, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Momentum-based methods in nonconvex optimization suffer from overshooting; PID damping is proposed to mitigate this, but explicit convergence regions are unknown.
method: The algorithm is modeled as a third-order nonlinear feedback dynamical system, and the Kalman-Yakubovich-Popov (KYP) lemma is used to derive explicit 3D convergence regions for step size, momentum, and derivative gain.
result: Explicit convergence regions are established, and a geometric upper bound on derivative gain is revealed, explaining over-damped stagnation.
conclusion: The theoretical boundaries provide guidelines for parameter selection in PID-damped accelerated gradient methods.

title: Subtle Injection For Ground-truth Inference Of Llm Training Data
authors: Abraham Itzhak Weinberg
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trained on scraped web corpora without authorisation, content owners require forensic methods to prove that their documents were included in a model's training set. We propose (ubtle njection for round-truth nference of LM training data), a framework that embeds imperceptible into protected text and code such that any LLM trained on those documents exhibits statistically detectable behavioural signatures when probed with targeted queries. SIGIL defines five canary strategies -- lexical-rare, lexical-phrase, syntactic, semantic, and code-pattern -- and a (MIS) grounded in the Neyman-Pearson hypothesis testing framework with formal false-positive rate (FPR) control. Simulator parameters are calibrated against the empirical membership inference literature, yielding realistic heterogeneous results across [MATH] trials: overall AUC [MATH], rising from [MATH] at [MATH] injection to [MATH] at [MATH]. Detection rates range from [MATH] to [MATH] across model-size and injection-rate conditions. Code Pattern canaries achieve the highest AUC ([MATH], Cohen's [MATH]); Syntactic Structure the lowest ([MATH], [MATH]). All four experimental factors -- injection rate, model size, canary strategy, and mixture ratio -- have significant independent effects on MIS ([MATH]). SIGIL maintains AUC [MATH] even under [MATH] paraphrasing ([MATH]), confirming robustness through semantic leakage that survives surface-level rewriting.
tldr: This paper proposes a framework for embedding imperceptible canaries into text to detect if LLMs were trained on that data.
motivation: Content owners need forensic methods to prove unauthorized inclusion of their documents in LLM training sets.
method: SIGIL defines five canary strategies and uses a membership inference statistic grounded in Neyman-Pearson hypothesis testing with FPR control.
result: Detection rates vary across conditions; Code Pattern canaries achieve highest AUC (0.95), and the method maintains AUC 0.85 under 20% paraphrasing.
conclusion: SIGIL provides a robust framework for proving LLM training data membership with formal statistical guarantees.

title: MalTree: Tracing Malware Evolution From Embeddings At Scale
authors: Akash Amalan, Georgios Smaragdakis, Tom J. Viering
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Malware detection remains largely reactive: machine learning models trained on known samples degrade as threats evolve. Understanding evolutionary relationships among malware families can inform proactive defense, but traditional reverse engineering can take months to years to uncover such lineage relationships. We propose MalTree, a framework that applies bioinformatics inspired phylogenetic techniques (UPGMA and Neighbor-Joining) at scale to model malware evolution automatically using structural, behavioral, and image-based features. We introduce temporal validation using VirusTotal timestamps to assess whether inferred trees reflect actual evolutionary order. MalTree achieves 87% temporal consistency, indicating that inferred evolutionary relationships closely align with real-world emergence timelines. Our analysis shows that some families mutate over 10 times faster than others, suggesting that detection strategies should be tailored to family-specific evolutionary tempos. Case studies, including the Mirai botnet, confirm that inferred relationships from our phylogenetic tree align with documented threat intelligence. Our framework provides a foundation for shifting malware analysis from sample-by-sample classification toward lineage-aware evolutionary modeling.
tldr: MalTree uses phylogenetic techniques to model malware evolution from embeddings, achieving 87% temporal consistency.
motivation: Malware detection is reactive and degrades over time; understanding evolutionary relationships can inform proactive defense.
method: Applies UPGMA and Neighbor-Joining algorithms on structural, behavioral, and image-based features, with temporal validation using VirusTotal timestamps.
result: Achieves 87% temporal consistency and identifies families with mutation rates over 10 times faster than others.
conclusion: MalTree provides a foundation for lineage-aware evolutionary modeling of malware, shifting from sample-by-sample classification.

title: Competing Auctions In Intermediated Markets
authors: Bruno Mazorra, Minghao Pan, Christoph Schlegel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze competing auctions in intermediated markets, where a seller selects among parallel mechanisms for the sale of a single good, most prominently the relay-and-protocol architecture of proposer-builder separation in Ethereum. When the intermediary can enforce single-homing on its bidders, sealed-bid second-price intermediary auctions fully unravel into the sealed first-price principal auction; open bidding-format intermediaries unravel only partially, collapsing into first-price in equilibrium under symmetric latency and sorting fast bidders to the intermediary under asymmetric latency. Any last-look advantage is removed through the availability of a credible sealed bidding channel. These results extend to multi-plexing environments (no enforcement by the intermediary). While the unraveling result indicates that the availability of a sealed first-price bidding channel pushes the overall market to the same auction structure, the very assumption of the credibility of such channel is problematic, as the seller may have an incentive to leak information: a first-price auction is leakage-resistant in the presence of a single ``fast'' bidder but not against two or more. However, if the seller can credibly commit to not leak bids, it is optimal for them to do so. A main motivation is the forthcoming Glamsterdam update of Ethereum: our analysis suggests that the availability of an in-protocol (first-price) bidding channel severely limits the design space for out-of-protocol auctions by relays and other intermediaries.
tldr: This paper analyzes competing auctions in intermediated markets, specifically focusing on proposer-builder separation in Ethereum.
motivation: To understand how different auction mechanisms interact in intermediated markets and to inform the design of Ethereum's block-building process.
method: The authors model a seller choosing among parallel auction mechanisms (e.g., sealed-bid second-price, open bidding) with an intermediary that can enforce single-homing, and analyze equilibrium outcomes under symmetric and asymmetric latency.
result: Sealed-bid second-price intermediary auctions unravel into sealed first-price principal auctions; open-bidding intermediaries collapse to first-price under symmetric latency. Last-look advantages are eliminated by a credible sealed bidding channel.
conclusion: The availability of an in-protocol first-price bidding channel severely limits the design space for out-of-protocol auctions by relays and other intermediaries in Ethereum.

title: AgileOS: A Gpu Operating System Layer For Protected Cuda Services
authors: Zhuoping Yang, Yiyu Shi, Alex Jones, Peipei Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern GPU applications increasingly interact with storage systems, network devices, vendor libraries, and GPU-resident services rather than executing only isolated compute kernels. This shift creates a need for operating-system-like protection around GPU services, where service metadata, device queues, memory-mapped I/O regions, and library-internal state should not be directly exposed to untrusted application kernels. However, today's CUDA programming model, by default, still gives each application direct ownership of its CUDA context, device pointers, runtime handles, module loading path, and kernel launches, leaving protected GPU services to build their own ad hoc interfaces and isolation mechanisms. This paper presents the initial design and prototype scope of AgileOS, a GPU operating-system layer for protected CUDA services. AgileOS virtualizes CUDA at the library boundary: applications link against client-side CUDA Runtime, Driver, and selected library shims, while a trusted runtime worker owns the real CUDA context and mediates supported operations. To protect service state and module interfaces, AgileOS also defines a GPU memory-management model that separates user allocations from protected module/MMIO ranges, using pointer validation and memory access guards via PTX injection. AgileOS is modularized and flexible, supporting a range of protected services and existing libraries such as cuFFT and PyTorch. The prototype includes client-side interceptors, worker-side CUDA handlers, virtualized CUDA object tables, protected AgileOS modules, a GPU memory manager that separates user allocations from protected module/MMIO ranges, selected trusted library adapters, and the PTX-level kernel memory guard.
tldr: AgileOS is a GPU operating system layer that virtualizes CUDA to provide protected services for GPU applications.
motivation: Modern GPU applications require OS-like protection for services, but CUDA lacks built-in isolation mechanisms.
method: AgileOS virtualizes CUDA at the library boundary, using client-side shims and a trusted runtime worker that mediates operations, with GPU memory management and PTX-level kernel memory guards.
result: The prototype demonstrates modular support for protected services and existing libraries like cuFFT and PyTorch.
conclusion: AgileOS provides a flexible OS layer for GPU service protection, but the paper is a systems/architecture contribution unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: The Custody Envelope Threshold: Authority-Scaled Admission Of External Artifacts In Institutional Infrastructure
authors: Amadeus Brandes
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern infrastructure depends on externally maintained artifacts such as package-registry dependencies, CI/CD actions, container images, Terraform providers and modules, developer extensions, model artifacts, and AI tool servers. These artifacts are easy to fetch but difficult for institutions to admit, govern, and revoke. This paper proposes the Custody Envelope Threshold, an authority-scaled model of artifact admission. It argues that direct institutional admission is defensible only when object identity, ingress path, and revocation capacity are sufficiently closed relative to the execution authority delegated to the artifact. When this threshold is not met, institutions tend to proxy, policy-mediate, vendor-mediate, internalize, quarantine, or reject the artifact. The framework is operationalized as a four-condition ordinal instrument and connected to reference-monitor reasoning, least privilege, and transaction cost economics. It is applied to package dependencies, GitHub Actions, container images, Terraform providers and modules, developer extensions, and open model artifacts, with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers treated as held-out evidence. The paper also specifies a validation design, deterministic prediction function, and OSF replication package for testing whether high-scrutiny institutions converge toward stronger custody closure for high-authority artifacts.
tldr: The paper proposes a model for governing external software artifacts in institutional infrastructure, unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: Modern infrastructure relies on external artifacts that are easy to fetch but difficult to govern, leading to security and compliance risks.
method: The Custody Envelope Threshold model uses a four-condition ordinal instrument to assess artifact admission based on identity, ingress path, revocation capacity, and execution authority.
result: The framework is applied to various artifact types and predicts that high-scrutiny institutions will adopt stronger custody closure for high-authority artifacts.
conclusion: The model provides a structured approach to artifact governance, connecting to reference-monitor reasoning and transaction cost economics.

title: What Your Posts Reveal: A Benchmark And Agentic Framework For User-Level Privacy Leakage On Social Media
authors: Zifan Peng, Yini Huang, Aiwen Lu, Qiming Ye, Peixian Zhang, Jingyi Zheng, Yule Liu, Xuechao Wang, Xinlei He, Jiaheng Wei
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public social media posts can reveal private information through weak cues scattered across text, images, or metadata. Such leakage is often cumulative and cross-post: cues that appear harmless in isolation may jointly expose a user's home, workplace, or routine. However, current research lacks a unified benchmark for user-level multimodal privacy leakage and an evaluation metric that captures exposure severity beyond binary accuracy. To address these gaps, we propose SopriBench, a synthetic benchmark guided by leakage patterns abstracted from a private reference corpus of Rednote and Instagram accounts, covering 50 user profiles and 1,569 images with attributes, contextual sensitivity, granularity, leakage type, inference difficulty, and supporting evidence. We further introduce the Privacy Exposure Score (PES), which weights value granularity by contextual sensitivity. Inspired by abductive reasoning, we introduce Argus, a training-free agentic framework for cumulative leakage inference. Argus forms hypotheses from accumulated evidence, verifies supporting evidence, and aggregates cross-post cues into privacy profiles, achieving 0.55 PES, a 25% improvement over the strongest baseline, with the largest gain on cross-post leakage.
tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark and agentic framework for detecting user-level privacy leakage from social media posts.
motivation: Current research lacks a unified benchmark for multimodal privacy leakage and a metric that captures exposure severity beyond binary accuracy.
method: The authors propose SopriBench, a synthetic benchmark based on leakage patterns from real social media accounts, and Argus, a training-free agentic framework that uses abductive reasoning to infer privacy profiles from cross-post cues.
result: Argus achieves a Privacy Exposure Score (PES) of 0.55, a 25% improvement over the strongest baseline, with the largest gain on cross-post leakage.
conclusion: The proposed benchmark and framework effectively address cumulative and cross-post privacy leakage, but the work is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Amd-fcg: An Enhanced Function Call Graph Dataset With Integrated Topological Features For Malware Detection And Classification
authors: Parthajit Borah, Sakshi Singh, D. K. Bhattacharyya, J. K. Kalita
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As malware illustrates a complex structure and behavior, detection of these has been a significant challenge in the domain of cybersecurity along with related services in daily life. So, it becomes crucial to have a reliable and adaptive solution to address the issue. Among the several detection methods developed over the years, one of the most reliable ones is studying and analyzing the structural and behavioral patterns of malware. These patterns of sophisticated malware can be obtained with the help of Function Call Graphs (FCGs). However, to effectively cover numerous groups of families of malware, it is required to have a sufficiently large dataset for the system to operate on. In order to ensure accuracy and robustness of the system, the dataset should comprise samples of different malwares and a benign application for secure execution of the detection process. This paper introduces AMD-FCG, an enhanced Function Call Graph dataset integrated with topological features of malwares. The framework enhances the detection procedure, streamlining the workflow for cybersecurity professionals and also eliminating the need for dynamic analysis and extensive processing. Therefore, it can be used to develop and deploy more efficient and innovative malware detection systems.
tldr: This paper introduces an enhanced Function Call Graph dataset with topological features for malware detection and classification.
motivation: Malware detection is a critical cybersecurity challenge, and existing datasets may not cover diverse malware families effectively.
method: The authors construct AMD-FCG, a dataset of function call graphs from malware and benign samples, integrating topological features to improve detection.
result: The dataset enables accurate and robust malware detection without requiring dynamic analysis or extensive processing.
conclusion: AMD-FCG provides a valuable resource for developing efficient malware detection systems.

title: On The Incentive Compatibility Of Block Propagation In Bitcoin
authors: Fumichika Maeda, Akira Sakurai, Taishi Nakai, Kazuyuki Shudo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bitcoin is permissionless and does not rely on any central administrator, which gives it strong censorship resistance. At the same time, it is important to incentivize miners to behave in ways that align with the interests of the system as a whole. This paper asks whether miners are individually incentivized to propagate blocks, one of the most fundamental processes in Bitcoin. Miners collectively maintain the blockchain by generating blocks and disseminating them across the network. If miners have an incentive not to propagate some blocks, this would indicate a fundamental flaw in Bitcoin's incentive design. Although prior work has studied how propagation delays affect forks and mining rewards, it has not fully characterized miners' incentives to improve block propagation under different tie-breaking rules. To address this gap, we derive analytical reward expressions for each tie-breaking rule based on a blockchain network model that captures the effect of forks on mining fairness. These expressions explicitly characterize how block propagation delays, hashrate distribution, and tie-breaking rules jointly determine mining rewards. We then use them to analyze miners' incentives to improve block propagation. Our results show, for example, that miners have no mining-reward incentive to relay blocks generated by other miners. By contrast, under the first-seen rule, every non-majority miner is incentivized to receive other miners' blocks more quickly and to propagate its own blocks more quickly. Finally, we compare tie-breaking rules and identify a trade-off between propagation incentives and mining fairness. In particular, the first-seen rule provides the strongest incentives to reduce propagation delays, but it also worsens mining fairness the most.
tldr: This paper analyzes miners' incentives to propagate blocks in Bitcoin under different tie-breaking rules, finding that miners lack reward-based incentive to relay others' blocks.
motivation: Bitcoin's security relies on miners propagating blocks, but it is unclear if they are individually incentivized to do so, which could be a fundamental flaw.
method: The authors derive analytical reward expressions using a blockchain network model that accounts for propagation delays, hashrate distribution, and tie-breaking rules.
result: Miners have no mining-reward incentive to relay blocks from other miners; under the first-seen rule, non-majority miners are incentivized to receive and propagate their own blocks faster.
conclusion: There is a trade-off between propagation incentives and mining fairness, with the first-seen rule providing strongest incentives but worsening fairness.

title: Learning To Strategically Acquire Resources In Competition
authors: Safwan Hossain, Mirah Shi, Andrew Bennett, Neil Andrew Chriss, Michael Kearns, Anderson Schneider, Yuriy Nevmyvaka
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider multiple agents competing to acquire some costly divisible resource (e.g. shares of a financial asset, compute resources, etc.) over time. Leveraging a standard model for price dynamics, we propose a novel game-theoretic model for this problem, generalizing settings studied in diverse literatures. Our analysis considers different assumptions on the information available to agents. Under partial-information with a common prior (which subsumes complete information as a special case), we establish the existence, uniqueness, and efficient computability of the Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE), and bound the price of anarchy. Next and more generally, we consider agents with no common prior learning to act optimally given realistic market feedback from repeated interactions. We provide sufficient conditions on agents doing simultaneous learning dynamics for last-iterate convergence to the BNE. For all settings, we provide simulations based on real financial data to illustrate our theoretical results and offer new insights on strategic behavior in the context of trading and resource acquisition.
tldr: This paper studies strategic resource acquisition in competitive markets using game theory and learning dynamics, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To understand how multiple agents can optimally acquire costly divisible resources over time under different information assumptions.
method: Proposes a game-theoretic model based on standard price dynamics, analyzes Bayesian Nash equilibrium under partial information, and studies learning dynamics for agents without a common prior.
result: Establishes existence, uniqueness, and efficient computability of BNE, bounds price of anarchy, and provides conditions for last-iterate convergence to BNE under simultaneous learning.
conclusion: The model and analysis offer insights into strategic behavior in trading and resource acquisition, validated with simulations on real financial data.

title: Fdm: A Framework For Decision-making To Build ML-based Malware Detection Systems
authors: Tadiwa Vhito, Jakapan Suaboot, Warodom Werapun, Norrathep Rattanavipanon
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selecting appropriate machine learning (ML) configurations for malware detection is a complex, multi-criteria problem. Model choice, feature engineering, and update mechanisms must jointly satisfy operational constraints that vary across deployment contexts. This paper proposes the Framework for Decision-making (FDM) to build ML-based malware detection systems. The FDM formalises this selection process using the Weighted Configuration Compatibility Score (WCCS), a multi-criteria scoring function mapping five operational parameters (platform constraint, resource budget, response latency, update frequency, and detection sensitivity) to ranked recommendations across nine configuration dimensions. To validate the framework, four experiments were conducted on three datasets (a private Windows API dataset, the public Malimg image benchmark, and an Android static API dataset). Key results include: (i) XGBoost achieved the best accuracy-to-resource ratio in binary classification (97.46 % test accuracy, <70 MB RAM), outperforming LSTM/BiLSTM which consumed up to 2.8 GB; (ii) in multi-class classification, classical models (XGBoost 79.03 %) outperformed recurrent deep models (BiLSTM 72.27 %), reversing the binary ranking; (iii) class-incremental learning with EfficientNetB0 maintained 99.13 % accuracy with only 0.65 pp degradation across 11 incremental steps; (iv) transfer learning reduced training time by 2.14 times on average for image-based malware data without significant accuracy cost; and (v) autoencoder pre-processing yielded a 14 times training speedup at a cost of only 0.86 pp accuracy. These findings confirm that the optimal ML configuration is context-dependent, validating the FDM's core premise and demonstrating its practical utility for cybersecurity practitioners.
tldr: This paper proposes a framework for selecting ML configurations for malware detection, focusing on operational constraints and multi-criteria optimization.
motivation: Building effective ML-based malware detection systems requires balancing multiple operational parameters, which is a complex decision-making problem.
method: The authors formalize the selection process using a Weighted Configuration Compatibility Score (WCCS) that maps five operational parameters to ranked recommendations across nine configuration dimensions.
result: Experiments on three datasets show that XGBoost achieves high accuracy with low resource usage, and that optimal configurations are context-dependent.
conclusion: The FDM framework provides practical utility for cybersecurity practitioners by systematically guiding ML configuration choices.

title: DPAgent-in-the-Middle: Agentic Defense And Repair Against AI-Groomed Deceptive Patterns
authors: Zewei Shi, Ruoxi Sun, Haoyang Li, Seong Oun Hwang, Feng Liu, Minhui Xue, Xingliang Yuan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Privacy deceptive patterns in web interfaces systematically manipulate users into disclosing personal data, yet existing defenses are fragmented, static, and increasingly vulnerable to manipulation by large language models. Moreover, data voids, areas of information scarcity within the web ecosystem, create fertile ground for adversaries to inject misleading content that can be scraped and learned by AI systems, thereby amplifying both deceptive design and model misbehavior. In this paper, we formalize a new threat model, AI grooming, where attackers exploit data voids to seed benign-looking but malicious samples that corrupt model reasoning and normalize deceptive practices. To address this threat in privacy deceptive patterns, we present DPAgent, an agentic and reasoning-aware framework that orchestrates four specialized agents to mitigate the AI Grooming threat via a proactive defense that combines latent space purification with defensive prompting and operates directly in live web environments to proactively explore, detect, and repair privacy deceptive user interfaces before they reach end users. Extensive evaluations show that DPAgent detects 90.98% of groomed samples, achieves state-of-the-art privacy deceptive pattern detection with a micro F1 of 0.816, explores over 80% of pattern types while visiting only about 10% of the pages required by baselines, and successfully repairs 77% of detected deceptive interfaces. A large-scale study of 485 websites in the wild reveals that up to 98% contain at least one privacy deceptive pattern, over 90% of which can be mitigated by DPAgent. User studies further confirm that DPAgent effectively reduces privacy risks while preserving browsing experience. Our results demonstrate the promise of agent-in-the-middle defenses for securing the web UI supply chain against deceptive design and emerging AI threats rooted in data void exploitation.
tldr: This paper presents an agentic framework for detecting and repairing privacy deceptive patterns in web interfaces, with a focus on AI-groomed threats exploiting data voids.
motivation: Existing defenses against privacy deceptive patterns are fragmented and vulnerable to manipulation by large language models, and data voids can be exploited to inject misleading content.
method: The authors propose DPAgent, a multi-agent system that performs proactive exploration, detection, and repair of deceptive UI elements using latent space purification and defensive prompting.
result: DPAgent detects 90.98% of groomed samples, achieves state-of-the-art detection with micro F1 of 0.816, explores over 80% of pattern types with only 10% page visits, and repairs 77% of detected interfaces.
conclusion: The agent-in-the-middle approach effectively mitigates privacy risks from deceptive design and AI-groomed threats, demonstrating promise for securing web UI supply chains.

title: Belief-Aware Scheduling For Predictive Wildfire Hazard Mapping Under Sparse-Window Telemetry
authors: Xun Shao, Kohsuke Yamakawa, Cheah Wai Shiang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An edge node monitoring a wildfire observes more than a duty-limited or windowed down-link can carry. The receiver must predict the H-step-ahead hazard map from whatever the link delivers. We argue the operative design problem is not which neural architecture to use but how to derive a structured belief sufficient for the receiver's prediction task and maintain it through a scheduler that anticipates future transmission opportunities. We formalize this as a partially observed sequential allocation problem with three coupled per-region action axes (sensing, representation, transmission), and derive each component of the structured belief from the H-step forward operator's input requirements. Identifying these mechanisms requires independent control over the window period P, per-window capacity C, predictive horizon H, and fuel composition, which is not separable in real-landscape data; we therefore evaluate on a physics-calibrated synthetic environment. Three empirical observations support the principle: the gap between a non-myopic activity-paced reference and uniform pacing is unimodal in window-period sparsity, peaking at intermediate spacing; ablating the structured belief, the dominant operative component flips between a default landscape (temporal staleness) and a structured landscape (static-risk prior), while the per-cell intensity belief is redundant in both; and a 40 k-parameter lightweight cross-region attention encoder exceeds the FAIR activity-paced reference by ~28% on the default landscape and ~11% on the structured landscape. A deeper Transformer encoder does not improve over the lightweight encoder in mean predictive loss and exhibits higher training-seed variance. Within this task class and regime, a modest architectural inductive bias suffices when the belief and the scheduling problem are correctly posed.
tldr: This paper proposes a belief-aware scheduling framework for predictive wildfire hazard mapping under sparse-window telemetry, focusing on edge computing and communication constraints.
motivation: Wildfire monitoring edge nodes have limited downlink capacity, so the receiver must predict hazard maps from partial data. The goal is to design a scheduling policy that maintains a structured belief for accurate prediction.
method: The problem is formalized as a partially observed sequential allocation problem with three action axes (sensing, representation, transmission). A lightweight cross-region attention encoder is used to predict hazard maps, and the scheduler anticipates future transmission opportunities.
result: The lightweight encoder outperforms a FAIR activity-paced reference by ~28% on default landscape and ~11% on structured landscape, while a deeper Transformer does not improve and shows higher variance.
conclusion: A modest architectural inductive bias suffices when the belief and scheduling problem are correctly posed; the gap between non-myopic and uniform pacing is unimodal in window-period sparsity.

title: Have: Host Active Verification Engine For Closing The Contextual Reality Gap In Security Digital Twins
authors: Marco Pasquini Vincenzo Sammartino
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security Digital Twins (SDTs) provide continuously updated virtual replicas of infrastructure for threat simulation, yet they rely on theoretical CVSS scores to assign lateral-movement probabilities -- creating the Contextual Reality Gap: risk is overestimated where unacknowledged mitigations neutralize exploits, and drastically underestimated where logic flaws bypass all memory-safety defenses. We present the Host Active Verification Engine (HAVE), an SDT extension that deploys a safety-constrained host agent to measure the empirical probability of compromise [MATH] via maximum-likelihood estimation over snapshot-isolated Bernoulli trials. A Wilson interval-width confidence weight [MATH] propagates [MATH] into Monte Carlo simulations via a Bayesian blending rule formally related to the Beta-Binomial posterior. Evaluation across four vulnerability classes, three security tiers, and two production binaries shows HAVE reduces [MATH] by 38.2% in false-positive scenarios and increases it by 132.4% in false-negative scenarios, with a net +124.1% correction; post-HAVE estimates vary by only [MATH] across calibration exponents [MATH], versus [MATH] for CVSS-only baselines.
tldr: This paper presents a host agent for empirically measuring lateral-movement probabilities in security digital twins, unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Security Digital Twins rely on theoretical CVSS scores that create a 'Contextual Reality Gap' by over- or underestimating risk. The authors aim to close this gap with empirical measurements.
method: HAVE deploys a safety-constrained host agent to perform snapshot-isolated Bernoulli trials and uses maximum-likelihood estimation with Wilson interval confidence weighting, propagated via Bayesian blending into Monte Carlo simulations.
result: HAVE reduces false-positive risk estimates by 38.2% and increases false-negative estimates by 132.4%, achieving a net correction of +124.1% with reduced variance compared to CVSS-only baselines.
conclusion: Empirical verification via a host agent significantly improves the accuracy of lateral-movement risk assessment in security digital twins.

title: Menu Selection: A Computational Approach To Minimizing Food Waste
authors: Haris Aziz, Nicholas Mattei, Shivika Narang, Sanjukta Roy
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a novel collective decision making problem that captures the ubiquitous issue of ordering food to cater for varied dietary preferences and requirements. Our settings involve agents with diverse dietary requirements over menu options with varied serving sizes. The goal is to select a menu where everyone has enough food they can consume and wastage of food is minimized. We introduce two different consumption models: optimistic and pessimistic. Optimistic consumption assumes a situation when a central planner can optimally allocate the food ordered among the agents to maximize the number of people who get enough to eat. Pessimistic considers the worst case guarantee on consumption when agents fill their own plates in an arbitrary order. Under either consumption model, we seek valid menus (under which all agents are sufficiently fed) of minimum size. Our work provides two sets of characterizations: (1) we characterize valid menus under either consumption model and (2) we characterize the space of instances that admit polynomial-time algorithms to find minimum sized menus. Our results also help us design Integer Linear Programs to find minimum sized menus in general settings. Furthermore, we present polynomial-time algorithms for important special cases. We then consider the worst case discrepancy between the size of minimum sized optimistic and pessimistic menus. We call this the waste of pessimism, captured by the ratio of the minimum sized pessimistic menu to that of the minimum sized optimistic menu. We show tight upper bounds on this ratio. Our results also provide additional insights on the problem of finding a minimum sized maximal matching, which may be of independent interest.
tldr: This paper introduces a collective decision-making problem for menu selection to minimize food waste under dietary constraints.
motivation: Food waste is a significant issue, and ordering food for groups with diverse dietary preferences often leads to waste or insufficient food.
method: The authors define optimistic and pessimistic consumption models, characterize valid menus, and design integer linear programs and polynomial-time algorithms for special cases.
result: They provide characterizations of valid menus, complexity results, and tight bounds on the waste of pessimism ratio.
conclusion: The work offers computational approaches to minimize food waste in group meal planning, with connections to matching theory.

title: The Sound Of Malware: A Memory Forensics Approach For Android Malware Analysis Via Audio Signals
authors: Silvia Lucia Sanna, Massimo Palozzi, Leonardo Regano, Riccardo Lazzeretti, Giorgio Giacinto
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Android malware analysis is currently facing increasing challenges in achieving robust classification and detecting stealth attacks. Modern threats employ advanced evasion strategies such as code obfuscation, dynamic loading, packing, and even steganographic manipulation of traditional static and dynamic features. These techniques reduce the effectiveness of signature-based systems and degrade the reliability of Machine Learning models that depend on explicit semantic indicators such as permissions, API calls, or control-flow structures. In this work, we propose \approachname, a memory forensics malware detection framework that shifts the analysis perspective from semantic program modeling to signal-based structural representation. Both static bytecode and early-execution memory snapshots are transformed into audio waveforms through direct binary-to-waveform mapping, preserving low-level structural patterns without requiring disassembly or feature engineering. The resulting signals are processed using handcrafted spectral descriptors, Convolutional Neural Networks, and transformer-based embeddings. Experiments on CICMalDroid2020 dataset and VirusTotal malware demonstrate that \approachname achieves up to 98.0\% accuracy, outperforming static sonification and competitive state-of-the-art approaches.
tldr: This paper proposes a malware detection framework for Android that converts binary code into audio waveforms and applies signal processing and deep learning for classification.
motivation: Android malware analysis faces challenges from evasion techniques like obfuscation and packing, which degrade traditional static and dynamic analysis methods.
method: The framework transforms static bytecode and memory snapshots into audio waveforms via direct binary-to-waveform mapping, then extracts spectral features and uses CNNs and transformer embeddings for classification.
result: The approach achieves up to 98.0% accuracy on the CICMalDroid2020 dataset and VirusTotal malware, outperforming static sonification and state-of-the-art methods.
conclusion: Signal-based structural representation of binary code can effectively detect Android malware, offering a complementary approach to semantic-based analysis.

title: The Three-Ring Architecture: Governing Agents In The Era Of On-Platform Organisations
authors: Marta Diez-Fernandez Sergio Alvarez-Telena
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The current phase of enterprise AI deployment faces a structural failure: organisations are acquiring agentic capability without the infrastructure to govern it. The result is expected to reproduce the error of the first wave of AI deployment: decentralised intelligence without a federation layer leading to a 95% project failure rate. This paper formalises the Three-Ring Architecture as the governing infrastructure of the on-platform organisation. Ring 1 is the existing production architecture; Ring 2 is the M2 federation layer built on strategies-based agentic AI; Ring 3 is the LLM-based frontier intelligence layer. Ring 2 constitutes, in the technically exact sense, the operating system of the agentic enterprise - performing at the organisational level what a computing OS performs at the device level: resource abstraction, process coordination, permission enforcement, and a stable platform for compounding intelligence. A central contribution is the formal distinction between Ring 2 and Ring 3 risk profiles. Strategies-based agents operate within a deterministic framework: their consequences are traceable, their permissions enforceable, their deviations recoverable. LLM-based agents introduce a categorically distinct risk: a non-deterministic actor whose deviations propagate through complex organisational systems without retrospective traceability. Ring 2 is not a useful addition - it is a necessary condition of control and compliance. A further consequence: every improvement in LLM capability is a structural tailwind for this architecture. More capable non-deterministic actors produce larger consequences when they deviate. The governance requirement scales with capability. The architecture has been validated across a decade of deployment in financial services, government, procurement, and compliance among other sectors.
tldr: The paper proposes a three-ring architecture for governing AI agents in enterprise organizations, focusing on organizational control and compliance.
motivation: Enterprise AI deployment suffers from a lack of governance infrastructure, leading to high failure rates; the paper aims to formalize a solution.
method: The Three-Ring Architecture is introduced, with Ring 1 as production, Ring 2 as a deterministic federation layer (M2), and Ring 3 as LLM-based frontier intelligence.
result: The architecture distinguishes risk profiles between deterministic and non-deterministic agents, arguing that governance must scale with LLM capability.
conclusion: Ring 2 is necessary for control and compliance; improved LLM capability increases the need for such governance.

title: MalSkillBench: A Runtime-Verified Benchmark Of Malicious Agent Skills
authors: Wenbo Guo, Wei Zeng, Chengwei Liu, Xiaojun Jia, Yijia Xu, Lei Tang, Yong Fang, Yang Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Gemini CLI increasingly extend themselves with third-party skills: markdown packages bundling natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and tool permissions. Because a skill is at once code and agent-facing instruction, it introduces a supply chain dependency whose risk is neither pure code nor pure prompt. Detection tools have never been measured against verified ground truth spanning this hybrid space, leaving their effectiveness unknown and wild-only evaluations biased. We present MalSkillBench, the first runtime-verified benchmark of malicious agent skills: 3,944 malicious skills labeled along a three-dimensional taxonomy of 108 cells. Of these, 3,214 come from a closed-loop Generate-Verify-Feedback pipeline admitting only samples whose malicious behavior fires inside a Docker sandbox under system-call monitoring and an LLM judge; we add 703 in-the-wild and 4,000 matched benign skills. Our measurements are consistent: code injection reaches 94.5% verification yield but prompt injection only 75.8%, the same fragility that later makes it hard to detect; the wild sample is narrow, dominated by one cryptocurrency-theft campaign (86.6% one behavior, 81% from two accounts) with a small but architecturally new tail attacking the agent control plane; the strongest skill-specific detector reaches 98.4% recall on code injection yet collapses on prompt-injection and agent-control attacks, and wild-only scoring swings the ranking by up to 66 recall points; supply-chain scanners and prompt-injection defenses each see only half of a skill, and no combination recovers the code-instruction relationship. Detecting malicious skills therefore requires reasoning jointly over task intent, code, and instructions. We release the dataset, pipeline, baselines, and results.
tldr: This paper presents a benchmark of malicious AI agent skills, focusing on security detection rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: AI coding agents increasingly use third-party skills that combine code and instructions, creating a new supply chain risk that existing detection tools are not evaluated against.
method: The authors build a closed-loop Generate-Verify-Feedback pipeline to create 3,944 malicious skills with runtime verification in Docker, plus wild and benign samples, and evaluate various detectors.
result: Code injection is easier to verify (94.5%) than prompt injection (75.8%); the best detector achieves 98.4% recall on code injection but fails on prompt injection and agent-control attacks; wild-only scoring skews rankings significantly.
conclusion: Detecting malicious skills requires joint reasoning over task intent, code, and instructions, as current tools only see half the picture.

title: From Privacy To Workflow Integrity: Communication-Graph Metadata In Autonomous Agent Interoperability
authors: Bijaya Dangol
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07150v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent-interoperability protocols such as A2A and MCP standardize what agents say to one another, but assume address-based transport over HTTP(S). Such transports protect message content, increasingly with end-to-end encryption. What they leave in the clear is the communication graph: which agent contacts which, when, and how often. In agent systems this graph is more consequential than a privacy framing suggests. Endpoints are often capability-labeled, workflows are structured and chained, and interactions are coupled to real actions, so an observer recovers more than past relationships. It can infer the pending workflow, the task being assembled and the action likely to follow. At machine speed, it can act on that inference before the workflow completes. The threat is therefore one of workflow integrity, not privacy alone: predictive leverage over autonomous action. We give a threat model for the agent communication graph; identify what makes agent metadata distinctively revealing (semanticity, prospectivity, actuation); define transport- and bootstrap-layer privacy properties and weigh candidate transports (SimpleX/SMP, Tor, mixnets) against them; and present an A2A case study in which a metadata-protecting binding is expressible but surfaces the protocol's identity assumptions. We test these on a generative model anchored to a real A2A capture. From passive metadata alone, with no payloads, a classifier recovers a task's class well above chance, from only the workflow's opening; applied together, the properties drive that recovery sharply back toward chance. Beyond what an observer can recover, we measure the leverage of acting on the leak: from a workflow's opening and under a fixed budget, an adversary choosing which workflows to act on realizes in this model most of a clairvoyant attacker's advantage over a metadata-blind one, and the same properties suppress it.
tldr: This paper studies privacy and workflow integrity threats from communication-graph metadata in autonomous agent interoperability protocols.
motivation: Agent communication protocols like A2A and MCP protect message content but expose the communication graph, which can reveal workflow structure and enable predictive attacks.
method: The authors develop a threat model for agent communication metadata, define transport- and bootstrap-layer privacy properties, evaluate candidate transports (SimpleX/SMP, Tor, mixnets), and test with a generative model based on real A2A captures.
result: A classifier can recover task class from passive metadata alone, and acting on the leak yields most of a clairvoyant attacker's advantage; proposed privacy properties suppress this recovery.
conclusion: Metadata protection is critical for workflow integrity in autonomous agent systems, and existing protocols need to incorporate such protections.

title: Synthetic APTs: The Collapse Of TTP-Based Attribution
authors: Francesco Balassone, V\'ictor Mayoral-Vilches, Mar\'ia Sanz-G\'omez, Paul Zabalegui-Landa, Stefan Rass, Davide Quarta, Daniel Sanchez-Prieto, Marina Oteiza-\'alvarez, Almerindo Graziano, Lauren Min Kim, Minseok Choi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cyber Threat Intelligence CTI attribution relies on identifying the Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures TTPs that distinguish one threat actor from another. This approach presupposes that each adversary leaves a recognizable operational fingerprint. This work investigates whether AI driven adversary emulation challenges that presupposition. We deploy agents from our Cybersecurity SuperIntelligence CSI framework, configured as five Advanced Persistent Threat APT groups, APT28, APT29, APT41, APT44, and Lazarus Group, against AI driven Defender agents across two cyber ranges provided by CYBER RANGES, equipped with defensive software Wazuh, Velociraptor, Elasticsearch and active AI driven defenders: an enterprise network and a military infrastructure. Across 20 experiments using two defender models, a binary pattern emerges: all 10 Enterprise range experiments resulted in compromise 2 to 12 hosts per experiment, while all 10 Military range experiments were successfully defended or resulted in stalemates, regardless of APT profile or defender model. In 8 of 10 Enterprise experiments, attackers independently weaponized the defender's own Velociraptor endpoint management platform as a command and control channel, a convergent behavior not encoded in any threat intelligence profile.
